title: What Does SEER2 Mean When Replacing an AC?
h1: What Does SEER2 Mean When You're Replacing an Air Conditioner?
description: SEER2 is the newer efficiency rating for AC units and heat pumps, tested under tougher conditions. Learn what it means when replacing a system in California.
quick_answer: SEER2 is the updated efficiency rating for central air conditioners and heat pumps, used since 2023. It works like the old SEER rating, where a higher number means less electricity for the same cooling, but the test uses tougher airflow conditions that are closer to a real home. SEER2 numbers come out a bit lower than old SEER numbers for the same unit.
body:
If you're shopping for a new AC or heat pump, you'll see SEER2 on every quote and spec sheet. It's not a brand feature or an upgrade. It's simply the current way the efficiency of these systems is measured and labeled in the United States.

How is SEER2 different from SEER?

SEER stands for Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio. It compares how much cooling a system delivers over a season to how much electricity it uses. SEER2 measures the same thing, but the U.S. Department of Energy changed the test starting January 1, 2023.

The biggest change is airflow resistance. Real ductwork pushes back against the blower more than the old lab setup did. The SEER2 test uses higher external static pressure to reflect that, so the rating is closer to what a system does in an actual house. Because the test is tougher, the same equipment earns a slightly lower SEER2 number than its old SEER number.

That means you can't compare a SEER rating on your old unit directly with a SEER2 rating on a new one. A new 15 SEER2 system is a step up from an old 15 SEER unit, not the same thing.

What is the minimum SEER2 in California?

California is in the federal Southwest region, which has stricter minimums for central air conditioners than the northern states. For new split-system central ACs under 45,000 Btu/h, the minimum is 14.3 SEER2. Larger split ACs have a minimum of 13.8 SEER2. Split-system heat pumps have a national minimum of 14.3 SEER2.

The Southwest also has EER2 requirements for air conditioners. EER2 measures efficiency at a single hot test condition, which matters on the hottest inland days when the system runs flat out.

Is a higher SEER2 rating worth it in San Diego?

It depends on where you live and how much you run the AC. Here's a simple way to think about it:

  • Coastal homes with mild summers may run the AC only part of the year. A system near the minimum often makes sense, and the extra cost of a high-SEER2 model takes longer to pay back.
  • Inland homes that run the AC hard for months get more value from higher efficiency, since the savings add up every hot day.
  • Heat pump buyers should also look at HSPF2, the heating efficiency rating, since the system will be heating too.

Higher-SEER2 systems often use variable-speed or two-stage compressors. Beyond efficiency, they run longer at lower speeds, which usually means steadier temperatures, better humidity control and quieter operation.

What else affects real-world efficiency?

A high rating on paper doesn't guarantee low bills. Installation matters just as much. Things that pull real efficiency down include:

  1. A system that's the wrong size for the house
  2. Leaky or undersized ductwork, especially ducts in a hot attic
  3. Incorrect refrigerant charge
  4. Poor airflow from restrictive returns or dirty filters
  5. An outdoor unit that doesn't match the indoor coil

The SEER2 rating applies to a matched combination of outdoor unit and indoor coil or air handler. Make sure your quote lists a matched system.

How should I compare quotes?

Ask each contractor for the exact model numbers, the SEER2, EER2 and (for heat pumps) HSPF2 of the matched system, and whether a load calculation was done to size it. Ask what they'll do about the ductwork, since leaky ducts can waste much of what a high-efficiency system saves.

It also helps to ask how the new system will be set up after installation. A technician should confirm the refrigerant charge, measure airflow and check static pressure in the ducts. Those steps are what turn a good rating on paper into good performance in your home. If a quote skips them, ask why, because a rushed startup can cost you efficiency for the life of the system.

faqs: Do I have to replace my old AC because of SEER2?
No. SEER2 rules apply to new equipment being made and installed. Your existing system can keep running and be repaired as long as it's working.
Is 15 SEER2 the same as 15 SEER?
No. The SEER2 test is tougher, so a 15 SEER2 system is more efficient than an old system rated 15 SEER. You can't compare the two numbers directly.
EER2 measures efficiency at one hot outdoor temperature instead of over a whole season. It's a good indicator of how a system performs during heat waves, which matters for inland homes.
Does a higher SEER2 rating mean better comfort?

Often, yes. Higher-rated systems usually have two-stage or variable-speed compressors that run more steadily, which helps with even temperatures and humidity. Proper sizing and good ductwork still matter most.
